newsitem.title: CANADA: Report urges better deal for Canada natives.
newsitem.headline: Report urges better deal for Canada natives.

text.p: A Canadian government commission on Thursday urged more self-government and increased federal spending for Canada's aboriginal peoples and said failure to improve the plight of natives could lead to more violence.
The report by a special commission on aboriginal affairs said that continued failure by Canada to work out a fair relationship with aboriginal peoples "may well lead to violence."

The C$58 million (US$43 million) report, which took five years to complete, was commissioned after a 90-day standoff between Mohawk Indians and authorities at Oka, Quebec, in 1990. A policeman was killed in the standoff.
There were also confrontations last year between Indians and police at a provincial park in Ontario and in British Columbia. A native was shot to death by police in the Ontario incident.
The report recommended that Canada give aboriginals control of more land and resources and treat aboriginal governments as equal partners with the federal and provincial governments.
The commission also recommended the creation of a House of First Peoples, to join the House of Commons and the Senate in Canada's parliament.
Canadian Indian and Northern Affairs Minister Ron Irwin said the government would study the report's 440 recommendations, but he did not promise any legislation.
"The best way to approach it, is to look at the substance and the issues and then decide if this is the way we want to go," Irwin told a news conference.
Many of Canada's 810,000 Indians and Inuit (Eskimos) live in poverty and rely on federal assistance. They also have high rates of suicide and drug and alcohol abuse.

Natives represent less than three percent of the Canadian population, but account for 14 percent of inmates in federal prisons. Their life expectancy is about eight years shorter than that of other Canadians. The death rate of native babies is twice the national average.
The report was welcomed by native leaders who called it their only chance for a better future.
"This report represents the best chance we have in this century to offer hope for our people," Ovide Mercredi, National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations, told reporters.
The Assembly of First Nations represents most of Canada's Indians.
Earlier this year, Mercredi called for sovereignty for the aboriginal peoples, much like the independence sought by separatists in the French-speaking province of Quebec.
